<strong>Appui inconditionnel des projets: Unconditional support for mining projects, no ability to challenge inadequate consultations and paltry financial compensation: Innu band councils on the North Shore, elected amid turmoil, signed a historic agreement with the multinational Rio Tinto-IOC in December 2020, to the dismay of many members of their communities. In Matimekush-Lac John, residents were reportedly even promised $2,000 each to vote in favour of the project.
C’est la voix nouée par l’émotion que No: Normand Pilot, an Innu from Uashat mak Mani-utenam, tells us his story in a voice choked with emotion. It is not only his own story, but that of a legal proceeding that has affected his community for more than two years. In June 2019, he ran for councillor in the band council elections on Antonio Fontaine’s slate. The election did not bring his team to power, but that of the outgoing chief, Mike McKenzie. Pilot and other defeated candidates, including Bastien Roland Thirnish, who ran for chief, say they quickly noticed irregularities in the electoral process. “They started celebrating at 10 p.m., while the rest of us were still waiting for the results at 1 a.m.,” Pilot observed on election night.
Dans les jours qui ont suivi le vote, un: In the days after the vote, a team of about fifteen citizens and defeated candidates set about gathering the evidence that, for more than two years now, has underpinned the lawsuit challenging the council’s election. According to documents filed in court by Pilot’s team and reviewed by La Converse, ballot boxes from the advance vote were allegedly not sealed in accordance with the rules and were left unattended. In addition, ballots were allegedly falsified, and some votes were allegedly counted without representatives of both parties supervising. The documents also state that “several people were added to the voters’ list even though they were not eligible to vote.” In Pilot’s view, all of this confirms that there was electoral fraud in the June 26, 2019 vote.
Quelques mois après les élections, alors: A few months after the election, while the Uashat mak Mani-utenam council was still in turmoil over questions about the legitimacy of the process that had brought it to power, Chief Mike McKenzie and his team, along with the Matimekush-Lac John council, reached a historic agreement with the Iron Ore Company of Canada (IOC). The mining company has operated iron ore extraction sites on the Innu’s traditional territory for more than half a century. The agreement quashed a $900-million lawsuit filed by the Innu against IOC for damage done to the territory, and guarantees the supply of iron ore for the next 50 years, amounting to hundreds of millions of tonnes. Its scope is hard to grasp, and it has a direct bearing on many aspects of Indigenous life and culture, including the land, the notion of consent and the economy. For Pilot, who openly opposes the agreement, especially while the legitimacy of the sitting council is in question, the signatories held “all [his community’s] rights in their hands.”
L’entente, intitulée <em>Ussiniun</em>,: The agreement, called Ussiniun, which means “renewal” in Innu, was ratified in December 2020 and is presented as a way to advance reconciliation. But according to some Innu, it is instead the last nail in the coffin of the cultural heritage tied to their traditional territory, Nitassinan.
La communauté de Matimekush-Lac John est: The community of Matimekush-Lac John is located about 510 km north of the community of Uashat mak Mani-utenam. Illustration: Maya Sakkal
« [La population] ne sait pas ce qui est: “[People] don’t know what’s in it. Is it really good for our community and our future generations? Well, I don’t know,” wonders Martial Pinette about the agreement that his community co-signed. He has lived in Uashat mak Mani-utenam for a few years and is originally from Matimekush-Lac John, the other community that signed the agreement with IOC. As in Uashat mak Mani-utenam, the June 2019 election there generated plenty of controversy: the results naming Réal McKenzie chief were quickly challenged. An appeal committee ultimately recognized the legitimacy of his election in September 2020 and, three months later, he signed the document.Pinette would have liked to see the agreement with his own eyes to know what it says, but that wasn’t possible. “The council told me: ‘It’s confidential.’ I said I have the right to see that document, but they wanted me to travel to [Matimekush-Lac John]. That wasn’t possible for me; I’m in Sept-Îles for work,” he explains. “Even today, I have a lot of questions to ask.” George McKenzie, an Innu from Uashat mak Mani-utenam, took part in the consultations held in his community.
Mais comme pour M. Pinette, ses question: But like Pinette, he was left without answers to his questions. He says it was hard to get a straight story about the talks that took place. “The content of the consultation boiled down to four pages. I find that very condensed; we were far from seeing all of it,” he says.Hoping to answer the questions of the many Innu dissatisfied with the opacity of the agreement between their band councils and IOC, La Converse obtained a copy of the agreement, without its appendices, through a confidential source. We submitted it to an expert in Indigenous law to better understand the articles that make up its 40 pages.
Pour Me Nawel Hamidi, «ce manque de tran: According to Nawel Hamidi, “this lack of transparency is common in communities, because the band council concentrates all the power and there is no body overseeing the councils, other than the department of Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, based in Ottawa.” Illustration: Maya Sakkal
Pour Me Nawel Hamidi, ces 40 pages de l’: For lawyer Nawel Hamidi, the agreement’s 40 pages are riddled with clauses that disregard Canadian case law. “The abuse goes so far, it makes no sense,” says the outraged lawyer, who is involved in several Indigenous rights cases and is a doctoral candidate and member of the Human Rights Centre at the University of Essex, in England. “Not only is a billion-dollar lawsuit brought by the band councils of Matimekush-Lac John and Uashat mak Mani-utenam for the destruction of land in Nitassinan (unceded Innu territory) being cancelled, but [IOC] is also unilaterally giving itself the right to expand its infrastructure on the territory, to continue extractivism wherever the company decides, and with the requirement that community members support it in applications for operating permits. This is an agreement that takes First Peoples back almost a century when it comes to respect for their ancestral rights and self-determination,” says Hamidi, who sees it as an example of how “international corporations are kings and masters” on Indigenous territory.
La justice canadienne reconnaît l'import: Canadian courts recognize the importance of consent when it comes to industrial activity on Indigenous land. The Supreme Court of Canada’s Haida decision established in 2004 the duty to consult Indigenous communities affected by development projects. Yet one of the clauses of the Ussiniun agreement prevents the Innu from “claiming a failure by governments to satisfactorily fulfil their duty to consult them.” In other words, the Innu of Matimekush-Lac John and Uashat mak Mani-utenam cannot complain about an inadequate consultation process. “There’s a problem. It goes against Canadian law, against current case law,” the lawyer says again, outraged. And it doesn’t end there.Hamidi points out that one of the agreement’s articles forces the Innu to “fully support” all applications for mining titles, permits or authorizations made by IOC to governments from the time the agreement is signed. This clause runs counter to the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which guarantees Indigenous peoples free, prior and informed consent when decisions affecting their territory are made. What’s more, the agreement stipulates that the signatories release IOC from any claim for damages or losses that they “may or could assert” against IOC. “They’re exploiting the territory when they don’t even have the right to occupy it in this way, and the land claims aren’t even settled. It’s truly problematic,” says Hamidi.
Quant au manque de transparence auquel M: As for the lack of transparency Pinette faced when he tried to consult the agreement remotely, it is nothing new to Hamidi. She explains that “information circulates with difficulty in band councils” and that the agreement signed between the Innu and IOC is no exception. Photographing it or holding a digital copy is forbidden, and only certain council employees can access it. “Several members have tried to get a signed copy of the agreement, but the band councils don’t want to give out a signed copy,” Hamidi continues. In her view, this kind of situation is recurrent in many communities across Canada. “When we try to get copies of agreements, they refuse. They say it’s confidential,” she says. She explains this opacity by the fact that appendices, which sometimes include additional monetary clauses, are added to the signed version. “We often end up analyzing draft agreements,” she laments. For the lawyer, the territory to which the agreement applies is bewilderingly vague. “It may be deliberately nebulous: on the one hand, it says ‘the operating area is around Labrador City within a 40 km radius,’ while on the other, it says: ‘However, this agreement includes all future infrastructure and all future projects.’ […] Is that consent to exploit the [traditional Innu territory] whenever and wherever the corporation wants?” she asks. Indeed, Article 3.11 stipulates that IOC may carry out exploration work outside the 40 km area of interest, provided it is not in an area protected for its “significant cultural character.” Although IOC commits to consulting the Innu in order to take their concerns into account, under the agreement they have no recourse if they judge the consultation inadequate.
<strong>De 900 à 20 M$En 2013, les Innus: From $900 million to $20 millionIn 2013, the Innu of Matimekush-Lac John and Uashat mak Mani-utenam filed a $900-million lawsuit against IOC for violating their ancestral rights through its activities. The Ussiniun agreement cancels that lawsuit and sets out new financial terms between the parties. According to the documents La Converse reviewed, the settlement would instead be $20 million, paid immediately and split 50-50 between the two communities concerned. Annual royalties are also provided for based on the quantity of iron ore extracted from the ground, amounting to several million dollars for each community. Hamidi explains that “these funds are subject to the condition that they be reinvested mostly in IOC’s infrastructure and in that of the passenger train linking Sept-Îles and Schefferville” – the same railway IOC uses to ship its iron ore to the port of Sept-Îles.
George McKenzie explique, pour sa part,: George McKenzie, for his part, explains that it wasn’t easy for his community to access the information sessions, especially during the pandemic. “To register for the consultation, you had to go online. Our elders, I don’t think they can register like that,” he says. Because of the risks linked to COVID-19, which poses a greater danger to Indigenous communities due to overcrowded housing and pre-existing medical conditions, he says people didn’t mobilize. “There wasn’t much participation. […] I think it was the right time for the band council to push through an agreement like that,” he says.

Pour Me Hamidi, « ce manque de transpare: For Hamidi, “this lack of transparency is common in communities, because the band council concentrates all the power and there is no body overseeing the councils, other than the department of Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, based in Ottawa.” She says the pandemic made this opacity worse by limiting the gatherings where members could debate, reducing consultations, concentrating information online and restricting decision-making to virtual meetings. Some votes were even held virtually, which limited participation. Like George McKenzie, she points out that many elders and members don’t have the technology needed to take part in virtual meetings or simply to access information. Tshani Ambroise is the former chief of Matimekush-Lac John: he is the one who challenged the results of the 2019 election, which he lost to Réal McKenzie. He echoes George McKenzie. For him, “the consultations were not adequate.” “The content of the agreement wasn’t properly explained to the people. […] There was no openness to negotiation, to consultation, or even to the possibility of asking good questions,” he says. He also points out that $2,000 was promised to each family if the agreement was accepted. “To me, that’s flat-out buying votes to say yes in the referendum,” says the former chief, who had himself negotiated a similar agreement with IOC that was never ratified. Martial Pinette, the Matimekush-Lac John member who works outside his community, confirms he received the $2,000. “It was right before the holidays. That money came directly from the agreement with Rio Tinto,” he says. George McKenzie also says $2,000 was promised to each resident of Matimekush-Lac John if the agreement was accepted: “The economy [there] isn’t doing great. If you dangle $2,000 per vote, it doesn’t surprise me that band councils go about it that way. We’re at their mercy.” The residents of his own community, Uashat mak Mani-utenam, were not able to receive that sum.

Contactée au sujet de cette façon de pro: Contacted about this way of proceeding, Rio Tinto-IOC declined to comment and referred us to its press releases. The department of Crown-Indigenous Relations and the ministry responsible for Indigenous Affairs also declined to comment, citing respect for band council governance in these matters. The Uashat mak Mani-utenam band council did not respond to our repeated interview requests. At the time of writing, the Matimekush-Lac John band council had not responded to our interview request either.
Me Hamidi souligne qu’un désengagement p: Hamidi notes that political disengagement has been observable in some communities for several years. “There is very little participation in general assemblies, which leads to fairly significant governance problems,” she explains. She insists on putting this in context: it is a direct consequence of Canada’s colonial structure, which has sought for hundreds of years to destroy the self-determination of Indigenous peoples. “I call it a leaky canoe with a broken paddle. […] The structure is made that way, and we haven’t managed to get out of it,” adds Pierrot Ross-Tremblay, an Innu sociologist and Canada Research Chair in First Peoples’ Intellectual Traditions and Self-Determination.
Malgré ces difficultés, Normand Pilot ga: Despite these difficulties, Pilot is staying the course. “People often tell me I’m a sore loser. I’m not doing this because I didn’t win my election,” he says, visibly exasperated by the kind of comments he has been the target of since he started the legal action against Mike McKenzie’s council. “I’m doing this for my children and my grandchildren. For future generations. So that they have a legacy, [a future] where they can still assert their identity and practise [Innu] values and culture. To safeguard our language. That’s why I’m doing this,” he says, his voice breaking with emotion. At the time of writing, the lawsuit he filed is still not settled.
